input: Before Caelindra leaves, I look down at the page. "That sentence isn't in this draft. I finished with the keeper moving the sign. I agree with your principle, but I don't want to accept a correction to a line I didn't write." I keep my tone matter-of-fact and give her room to check the page. Then I put the manuscript safely on my desk, change into my dark formal coat with the signet and no sash, and head for the Chancellor's Hall in time for the reception.
output:
Caelindra stops with one hand on the doorframe. She takes the pages back and reads the final paragraph once, then again, checking the preceding page with increasing severity.

“No,” she says. “It is not there.”

The tips of her pointed ears darken. She lays the manuscript flat, as though accuracy might still be hiding in a crease.

“I expected an unnecessary explanation and mistook that expectation for ink.” Her formality becomes glacial. “That was careless. And patronizing. You were right to object.” She returns the pages. “I apologize. The ending requires no cut.”

Then she departs upstairs at a pace just short of flight.

By sixth bell, your manuscript rests safely on your desk and your inherited coat has replaced the mended charcoal one. Chancellor’s Hall gleams with white marble and tall storm-facing windows. Seven banners hang behind the receiving dais; the human standard is so newly unfolded that creases still cross its field.

Your classmates have become ceremonial versions of themselves. Ashara’s bandaged knuckles show beneath black formal cuffs. Rashid is arguing under his breath that this proves his point about surrender. Caelindra, silver hair elaborately pinned, meets your eye and gives you one precise nod.

Chancellor Ashworth comes to meet you before the bell’s final note fades. Age has softened his golden radiance to candlelight, but not his keen blue gaze.

“Master Garvey. Welcome to an institution your family helped build and frequently inconvenienced.”

Beside him stands a lean, brown-skinned man in an old-fashioned academic robe. His iron-grey hair is cut unevenly, and ink shadows two fingers.

“Professor Gareth Stone,” Ashworth says. “Our human historian.”

Stone begins a formal greeting. Then he sees your signet.

His words stop.

“That was Dan Garvey’s.” He leans nearer without touching your hand, his attention fixed on a small nick beside the engraved sheaf. Across the hall, Professor Windwhisper’s silver head turns almost imperceptibly.

Stone notices. His expression closes.

“I beg your pardon,” he says more quietly. “May I see the ring?”
